title: Placebos in dentistry: their profound potential effects.
journal: Journal of the American Dental Association (1939)
abstract: The placebo effect may influence the treatment of patients with postextraction pain, localized osteitis, and myofascial pain dysfunction syndrome, to name a few. The patient, the doctor, and the situation all influence the placebo effect. This phenomenon is still not understood, and further research is needed. The practitioner should learn to utilize the placebo effect for its potential benefits.

screening.rationale: Narrative discussion focused on placebo effects in dentistry and recommendations for clinicians, making placebo the main subject (review/opinion).

classification.summary: Discussed the potential influence of placebo effects in dental conditions, urged clinicians to utilize them and called for further research.

title: A critical look at the theory of placebo.

screening.rationale: Title indicates the paper is a theoretical/critical examination of placebo theory, meeting inclusion criterion 5 for placebo-science reviews/commentary.

classification.summary: Critically examined theoretical accounts, concepts, and assumptions underlying the placebo phenomenon.

title: Placebo: a place in medical therapy?
journal: The Journal of the Kentucky Medical Association

screening.rationale: Title explicitly addresses the role of placebo in medical therapy, indicating placebo is the paper's main subject despite no abstract being available.

classification.summary: Discusses the role and place of the placebo in medical therapy, including attitudes and risks, based on the paper's title.

title: Hypnosis: an informational approach.
journal: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences

screening.rationale: Title explicitly addresses hypnosis as an informational (mechanistic) account implicating suggestion/expectation processes relevant to placebo/nocebo mechanisms.

classification.summary: Proposed an information-processing account of hypnosis, focusing on suggestion and expectation as mechanisms influencing symptom reports and responses.

title: The powerful placebo.
journal: The New York journal of dentistry

screening.rationale: Title explicitly names placebo as the subject (‘The powerful placebo’), indicating the paper is about placebo phenomena rather than using placebo only as a comparator.

classification.summary: Discusses the potency and implications of the placebo phenomenon.

title: Patient characteristics and expectancy measures as factors that influence the expectancy-improvement relationship.
abstract: A recent study found factored measures of patient's expectancies for therapeutic gain significantly correlated with 1 of 15 objective measures of treatment outcome for the hospitalized patients. A subsequent study of the same relationship that used unfactored expectancy measured with a diagnostically homogenous sample of patients found the patients' expectancies significantly correlated with 10 of the same 15 measures of improvement. This study reexamined the initial expectancy-improvement data using unfactored measures of expectancy. The overall results showed that characteristics of samples of Ss and the adequacy of expectancy measures both significantly influence the results of tests of the expectancy-improvement relationship.

screening.rationale: Measured patient expectancies as predictors of therapeutic improvement (an expectancy–outcome relationship), which addresses placebo/expectation mechanisms per inclusion rules.

classification.summary: Reanalyzed expectancy–improvement data in hospitalized psychiatric patients and found that sample characteristics and adequacy of expectancy measures substantially influenced correlations between patient expectancies and treatment improvement.
classification.key_finding: Found that unfactored expectancy measures correlated with improvement on many outcome indices whereas factored measures showed far fewer correlations, indicating measurement and sample characteristics alter expectancy–outcome relationships.

title: Effects of alcoholics' expectation of a drink.
abstract: The expectation of receiving alcohol influenced the drinking behavior of alcoholics and social drinkers resulting in increases in the amount of placebo consumed and higher estimates by both alcoholics and social drinkers of the percentage of alcohol in the placebo.

screening.rationale: The study explicitly manipulated expectation about receiving alcohol and measured placebo consumption and perceived alcohol content, making placebo/expectation the paper's focus (experimental study of placebo effects).

classification.summary: Found that expecting alcohol increased placebo drinking and raised participants' estimates of alcohol percentage in the placebo.
classification.key_finding: Expectation increased amount of placebo consumed and raised perceived alcohol content in both alcoholics and social drinkers.

title: Placebos: a brief review for family physicians.
abstract: Placebos are as old as the practice of medicine and for thousands of years represented nearly the totality of medical therapeutics. Positive and negative placebo effects occur in about 35 percent and 10 percent of individuals, respectively. Without exception, all medical therapeutics may be assumed to have significant placebo components. Factors contributing to the success of placebos are many, but include the expectations of physician and patient, the doctor-patient relationship, and societal norms. Ethical issues regarding the use of placebos are not clear-cut but, in general, the use of placebos is contraindicated except as an adjunct to specific therapy, or as a research tool with informed consent.

screening.rationale: Narrative review whose main subject is placebo phenomena, ethics, prevalence and clinical factors, fitting 'placebo_science_other' inclusion (placebo as main subject).

classification.summary: Reviews ethical issues, reported prevalence, and contextual factors influencing placebo effects and advised limited use of placebos outside research or as adjuncts.

title: Effect of alcohol and benzodiazepines on performance as related to personality characteristics. Personality characteristics among healthy "placebo reactors" and nonreactors.
abstract: For 2 weeks 40 volunteers received either 5 mg diazepam, t.i.d., or 10 mg chlordiazepoxide, t.i.d., and placebo. A choice reaction test, two coordination tests, and an attention test were administered to the subjects on the 14th day of each treatment. Thirty minutes before the tests, the subjects ingested either alcohol., 5g/kg or a placebo drink, incombination with the last capsule. After the test the subjects rated the quality of their treatment as placebo, tranquilizer, or stimulant. The psychological tests taken before the treatments were Eysenck's EPIC-NESI, Taylor's Manifest Anxiety Scale (MAS), and Cattell's 16 PF inventory. A multiple regression analysis was computed. Personality factor scores found to be associated with a strong effect of the benzodiazepines were 16 PF's A, C, L, N, and Q, and EPIC's E. The effect of alcohol was associated with a high score of 16 PFs B factor. Personality factors associated with "placebo reactors" and nonreactors were investigated, as well. Those subjects on placebo indicating their treatment to be active were classified as "placebo reactors". A discriminant analysis revealed that 16PF's O and I factors discriminated effectively "placebo reactors" from nonreactors, and EPIC's SE and 16 PF's L factor nonreactors from "reactors".

screening.rationale: The paper explicitly analyzed predictors of being a 'placebo reactor' (placebo-arm responders) using personality measures, so placebo response was the object of study.

classification.summary: Analyzed healthy volunteers who received benzodiazepines, alcohol, or placebos and found personality factors that distinguished subjects who reported active effects while on placebo (placebo reactors) from nonreactors.
classification.key_finding: Discriminant analysis showed 16PF factors O and I (and EPIC scales) effectively distinguished placebo reactors from nonreactors; 40 participants were studied.

title: Patients' attitudes and attributions to electroconvulsive shock therapy.
abstract: An attributional analysis of ECT as a placebo was investigated by comparing the attitudes of patients on two psychiatric wards. It was hypothesized that on the ward on which ECT was administered more frequently, general attitudes toward the treatment would be more favorable and more patients would express the opinion that ECT had worked well for them personally. The results, which supported the predictions, indicate that the operation of placebo effects in connection with ECT may account for differential treatment results more adequately than explanations based on physiological models. The findings also suggest that more research is needed to explore the relationship between patients' attitudes and treatment outcomes.

screening.rationale: Study surveyed patient attitudes and attributions about ECT and discussed placebo explanations, fitting 'placebo science' (attitudes/attributions) inclusion rather than an experimental placebo-effect design.

classification.summary: Compared patient attitudes and attributions about ECT across two wards and argued that placebo processes may help explain differential perceived effectiveness.

title: Placebo versus allopurinol for renal calculi.
abstract: Certain patients with recurrent calcium oxalate calculi will show a mild uricacidemia and/or uricosuria. A prospective blind study was begun in 1970, comparing placebo to allopurinol in the management of these patients. The 92 patients had been followed for a minimum of 6 months to 5 years before the code was broken. It is demonstrated clearly that there is a placebo effect in the management of renal calculous disease. It also has been shown that the only event that clearly separates the 2 groups is complete cessation of calculous formation. Allopurinol is effective in 61 per cent of the patients and these successes usually can be identified after 1 year of treatment.

screening.rationale: Randomized, blinded trial explicitly reported and analyzed a placebo effect in management of renal calculi, so placebo response was a focus.

classification.summary: Randomized, double-blind trial (n=92) compared allopurinol to placebo in recurrent calcium oxalate stone formers and reported a clear placebo effect while allopurinol produced higher rates of complete cessation of stone formation.
classification.key_finding: Found a demonstrable placebo effect in management of renal calculi; allopurinol achieved complete cessation in ~61% of patients.

title: Gastric and duodenal ulcer healing under placebo treatment.
abstract: The healing time relation of 30 gastric and 15 duodenal ulcers was assessed by repeated endoscopic measurements of ulcer size on days 1, 21, and 42 of a 6-week period, during which a selected population of patients was being treated as outpatients on an inert placebo. Antacids in small amounts were only given in case of ulcer pain. There was evidence for a linear relationship between the absolute initial ulcer size and its reduction with the time in incompletely healed ulcers of both types. Their percentage reduction from the original size was 71% after 3 weeks in gastric and 83% in duodenal ulcers; 82% after 6 weeks in gastric and 83% in duodenal ulcers. The healing time course for both types of ulcers appeared to follow an exponential function. The calculated half-life was 1.7 weeks for gastric and 1.9 weeks for duodenal ulcers. The number of healed duodenal ulcers observed at the 3-week examination was significantly greater than that of healed gastric ulcers (P = 0.05). It is concluded that repeated measurements of the ulcer size before complete ulcer healing contribute to a optimal characterization of the healing time course. The calculated half-life of less than 2 weeks makes shorter control intervals reasonable for both types of ulcers. The ulcer half-life appears to be a more accurate criterion of the healing process than that of complete healing.

screening.rationale: Single-group outpatient study explicitly treated patients with an inert placebo and measured ulcer healing over time, so placebo response (change on placebo) was the object of study.

classification.summary: Treated 45 patients with gastric or duodenal ulcers with an inert placebo and measured endoscopic ulcer size over 6 weeks, finding substantial objective healing (half-life ~1.7–1.9 weeks).
classification.key_finding: Observed mean percentage reduction in ulcer size of ~71–83% by 3–6 weeks and estimated ulcer half-lives of 1.7 weeks (gastric) and 1.9 weeks (duodenal).

title: Placebo and its importance in medicine.
journal: International journal of clinical pharmacology and biopharmacy
abstract: Placebo can be defined as "a therapeutic effect, drug or non-drug, or a part of it which, in the condition being treated, objectively does not have any specific pharmacodynamic action." Even today when powerful drugs are available placebo is important and present in therapy. Effective therapeutic agents are also sometimes used as placebo, mostly inadvertently. In clinical pharmacological investigations placebos are used deliberately to discriminate the pharmacodynamic action of drugs from psychic and other factors which can influence the objective of the drug evalution. The use of placebo in therapeutic trials is justified only when no effective treatment is available or the symptom or disease is trivial. Placebo effect is especially pronounced in diseases where pain is an important symptom as well as in psychosomatic diseases. The extent of placebo reaction depends on patient's characteristics (reactors and non-reactors), drug presentation, as well as on personality and attitudes of the prescriber. Deliberate use of placebo other than in clinical therapeutic investigation is justified in mild mental depression and in situations where the diagnosis is known, no drug is necessary, but the patient's pressure to get a prescription is irresistible (?). Every doctor should cultivate the induction of placebo reaction in treatment of his patient, but not to the extent that the belief of the former in the action of an inactive medication starts.

screening.rationale: Paper is a narrative discussion of the role, ethics and clinical use of placebo, making placebo the main subject (placebo science/clinical use).

classification.summary: Discussed the definition, ethical considerations, and clinical importance of placebo effects and their determinants, arguing for cautious and limited therapeutic use.
classification.key_finding: Argued that placebo effects are clinically important—especially for pain and psychosomatic conditions—and depend on patient traits and prescriber behavior.

title: A clinical study of the use of human chorionic gonadotrophin in weight reduction.
abstract: Treatment of obesity with human chorionic gonadotrophin was shown to be of no better value than saline in a double-blind crossover study of weight reduction in obese subjects. There was also no significant difference in mood, hunger, or missed injections, and no apparent difference in adherence to diet when the two agents were compared. In contrast, a significant difference was found in the ability of subjects to lose weight in the first four weeks of the study in contrast with the second four weeks, no matter which agent was used. Thus, the initiation of a new therapeutic program, even using an inert agent, has a temporary benefit--a manifestation both of placebo effect and the Hawthorne effect.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind crossover trial that reported a placebo (saline) response/time-limited early benefit interpreted as a placebo/Hawthorne effect, making placebo response an explicit study finding.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind crossover trial found hCG was no better than saline for weight loss and observed greater weight loss in the first four weeks regardless of agent, interpreted as a placebo/Hawthorne effect.
classification.key_finding: Found no difference between hCG and saline; early greater weight loss in the first 4 weeks regardless of treatment, suggesting a transient placebo/Hawthorne response.

title: A note on the addictive personality: addiction to placebos.

screening.rationale: Title and indexing indicate the paper is a case report specifically about addiction to placebos, making placebo phenomena the primary subject.

classification.summary: Reported a clinical case of a patient exhibiting addictive use of placebos and associated euphoria.

title: The placebo effect. Is it important in diverticular disease?
abstract: Thirty patients with diverticular disease confirmed by barium enema examination were entered into a three-month double-blind trial of two tablets of methylcellulose (Celevac) daily or two placebo tablets daily. As these tablets were indistinguishable it was possible to cross over nine of the patients and follow them for a further three-month period. The placebo effect was sufficient for 11 patients who completed the trial on placebo to show a small mean improvement. A greater mean clinical improvement was shown, however, by the 16 patients who completed the trial on methylcellulose and in those who were crossed over, most of the improvement occurred during the time the patients were on methylcellulose.

screening.rationale: The trial explicitly examined the magnitude of improvement on placebo (placebo response) and compared it to active methylcellulose, with placebo response reported as a main finding.

classification.summary: Reported a double-blind methylcellulose versus placebo trial in 30 patients with diverticular disease and found a small mean improvement in patients on placebo but greater improvement on methylcellulose.
classification.key_finding: Found a small mean clinical improvement in the placebo group (11 completers) but larger improvement in the methylcellulose group (16 completers).

title: Conditioned insulin secretion and meal feeding in rats.
journal: Journal of comparative and physiological psychology
abstract: Previous researchers have reported that rats placed upon a feeding regimen such that they receive only 2 hr of food per day (meal-fed rats) develop hyperinsulinemia at the time of the day associated with feeding, even in the absence of food. Controls fed ad lib had no such response. In a series of several experiments, meal-fed rats had elevated insulin levels at only the specific time of the day associated with feeding, and the increment of insulin at that time could be eliminated with atropine. Free-feeding controls, on the other hand, always had higher insulin levels than the meal-fed rats, did not have an elevation of insulin at the time of the day that the meal-fed rats normally ate, and had insulin values that were unaffected by atropine. Further experimentation showed that hyperinsulinemia could become associated with arbitrary stimuli always associated with eating for meal-fed rats. It is concluded that the hyperinsulinemia of meal-fed rats associated with their feeding time is a learned response.

screening.rationale: Animal experiment that explicitly tested conditioned (learned) insulin secretion to feeding-associated cues, fitting placebo/nocebo mechanism research (classical conditioning) in nonhuman models.

classification.summary: Found that meal-fed rats developed conditioned anticipatory insulin release to feeding-associated cues, and that this hyperinsulinemia was abolished by atropine.
classification.key_finding: Meal-fed rats showed time- and cue-specific conditioned increases in insulin, which were eliminated by atropine, implicating learned cholinergic-mediated anticipatory secretion.

title: Differences in placebo effects.
abstract: Constant volume injections of water and saline were evaluated in terms of their effects upon locomotor activity in the rat. Both solutions produced an overall decrease in activity and were found to be nonequivalent in their effect.

screening.rationale: Animal experiment explicitly examined behavioral changes after inert injections (placebo vehicles), making placebo response the paper's focus.

classification.summary: Tested effects of constant-volume water and saline injections on rat locomotor activity and found both produced overall decreases in activity with non-equivalent effects.
classification.key_finding: Both inert injection vehicles (water and saline) reduced locomotor activity in rats, and their effects differed.

title: Placebos in psychiatric therapy.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly names placebos in psychiatric therapy, indicating placebo phenomena are the paper's main subject (review/discussion).

classification.summary: Reviews topics related to the use and role of placebos in psychiatric therapy.

title: Placebo effect of psychotropic drugs on patients and staff.
journal: Revue de neuropsychiatrie infantile et d'hygiene mentale de l'enfance

screening.rationale: Title explicitly names the 'Placebo effect' as the subject (placebo effects of psychotropic drugs on patients and staff).

classification.summary: Investigated placebo effects of psychotropic drugs on patients and clinical staff.

title: A study of the variations in the response regarding duodenal ulcer when treated with placebo by different investigators.
abstract: Four series of duodenal ulcer patients presenting with pain have been treated with two types of placebos (intramuscular injections or tablets) by 4 different physicians while a fifth group of patients did not receive any treatment. Patients noted the number of days with pain since the beginning of the test by themselves. All patients treated with placebo presented with a significantly shorter duration of pain than untreated patients. There was a significant difference between the actions of the different physicians on the duration of pain. This suggests that some, until now unprecised, character(s) of the physician plays an important part in the relief of duodenal ulcer pain.

screening.rationale: The study experimentally compared placebo treatments (tablets or injections) against an untreated group and analyzed physician-related differences in placebo-associated pain duration, making placebo response/effect the explicit focus.

classification.summary: Treated duodenal ulcer patients received placebo tablets or injections or no treatment; placebo groups had shorter pain duration and effects varied by treating physician.
classification.key_finding: Placebo-treated patients reported significantly shorter pain duration than untreated patients, with significant variation across physicians.

title: Morphine tolerance acquisition as an associative process.
journal: Journal of experimental psychology. Animal behavior processes
journal_abbrev: J Exp Psychol Anim Behav Process
abstract: The results of several experiments supported the proposal that morphine analgesic tolerance is a manifestation of an association between the drug administration ritual and the systemic effects of the drug: (a) Presenting environmental cues previously associated with morphine, but without the drug, attenuated established tolerance (i.e., morphine tolerance can be extinguished), (b) repeated presentations of the morphine administration procedure, prior to its pairing with the opiate, retarded the acquisition of tolerance (i.e., morphine tolerance is subject to "latent inhibition"), and (c) placebo sessions interspersed between morphine sessions deleteriously affected the development of tolerance (i.e., morphine tolerance is subject to the decremental effects of partial reinforcement). These findings appear inexplicable by most traditional theories of tolerance, which do not emphasize the role of drug-associated environmental cues in the development of tolerance. Additionally, it is suggested that the conditioning analysis of tolerance is congenial with a current view of habituation, and there may be a similar associative basis for the response decrement to both endogenous and exogenous iterative stimulation.

screening.rationale: Animal experiments explicitly tested associative (placebo-like) cue presentations and placebo sessions affecting morphine tolerance, meeting inclusion rule for animal models with cue/context contrasts.

classification.summary: Found that morphine analgesic tolerance in rats was shaped by associative cues: cue-only (placebo) sessions attenuated tolerance, latent inhibition slowed tolerance acquisition, and partial reinforcement reduced tolerance development.
classification.key_finding: Presenting morphine-associated cues without drug attenuated established tolerance and placebo (cue-only) sessions disrupted acquisition of morphine tolerance.

title: EEG feedback training in the treatment of epilepsy: some questions and some answers.
journal: The Pavlovian journal of biological science
abstract: A basic question in EEG feedback training of epileptic patients is whether the decrease in seizures is specifically due to the training or to other factors. Questions may also be raised as to what EEG changes are involved. Preliminary results in five patients suggest that seizure reductions can occur with training which are not due to placebo or nonspecific effects or to changes in medication compliance. These changes occurred rapidly during EEG-contingent feedback training but not when feedback was random in relation to the EEG. Reliable changes in the EEG were also observed, but the question of which mechanism accounts for these results has yet to be answered.

screening.rationale: Experimental EEG-contingent feedback was contrasted with random feedback to test whether seizure reductions were due to specific training rather than placebo/nonspecific effects, making placebo mechanisms an explicit focus.

classification.summary: Reported preliminary results in five epilepsy patients showing seizure reductions and reliable EEG changes during EEG-contingent feedback training but not during random feedback, suggesting effects beyond nonspecific/placebo factors.
classification.key_finding: Seizure reductions occurred rapidly with EEG-contingent feedback but not with random feedback, alongside reliable EEG changes.
